podcasts.name: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grammy Award Category Introduction (1991)
podcast.body: The "Alternative Album" category was first introduced at the Grammy Awards in 1991, years after alternative albums began to gain prominence. This marked a significant moment of formal recognition for the genre by the Recording Academy. "It wasn't until 1991 that the genre had its own category."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Ongoing History Book of Firsts

podcast.title: Mainstream Breakthrough in 1991
podcast.body: Alternative rock had existed in a parallel universe for at least 15 years, but in 1991, the barrier collapsed, and it flooded into the mainstream. This shift was so significant that by the end of the year, alternative rock effectively ceased to be alternative, becoming the mainstream. "But in 1991, the barrier between the two rock universes collapsed. And alternative rock flooded into the mainstream."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: End of Boom (1996)
podcast.body: By 1996, the boom period for alternative rock had largely concluded, leading to an era dominated by pop music. "By 1996, the boom in Alt Rock had run its course, and the world slipped into an era where pop music ruled."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Struggles in 2000
podcast.body: At the turn of the millennium, Alt Rock "had apparently reached some kind of a dead end," with grunge heroes either having broken up, moved on, or died, and New Metal being too polarizing to carry the genre. "Rock, especially Alt Rock, had apparently reached some kind of a dead end."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: History Series Context (2010)
podcast.body: A 15-part deep dive into the history of alternative rock, titled "the history of alt-rock series," was produced, examining every facet of alt-rock from the 1950s up to the present day. "a 15-part deep dive into the history of alternative rockets, the history of alt-rock series."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Alt Rock Godfathers"
podcast.body: For a brief period around the launch of the Modern Rock Chart, artists like Graham Parker and Joe Jackson were welcomed at Modern Rock Radio as "alternative Godfathers." Elvis Costello went on to become the "copy" of these figures, topping the chart in its first year. "For a brief time, Parker was welcomed at Modern Rock Radio as a kind of alternative Godfather."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Alt Rock (North America) vs Indie (UK) – Same Thing, Different Words
podcast.body: The term "alternative" evolved in North America from FM radio stations in the 1970s that played slightly different music from corporate rock stations (an "alternative" to Journey, Styx, and Boston), and from bands who recorded for independent labels because major labels wouldn't have them. Campus radio stations spread the term. In the UK, the exact same thing was called "Indie," because these bands recorded for independent labels. Both terms describe left-of-center rock that descends not from the Beatles/Stones/Led Zeppelin lineage but from Iggy Pop, Bowie, the Velvet Underground, and the Ramones. "Same say, in North America these artists recorded for independent labels that were an alternative to the mainstream, hence it was alternative music. In the UK these artists recorded for Indy labels."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anticipated by David Bowie
podcast.body: David Bowie is credited with anticipating the rise of alternative rock, predating and influencing artists such as Nirvana and Nine Inch Nails. "who anticipated the video era as well as alternative rock."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Billboard's First Alt Rock Chart
podcast.body: Billboard launched its Modern Rock Tracks chart, the magazine's first Alt Rock Chart, in September of 1988. This marked a significant institutional recognition of the burgeoning alternative rock genre and provided a new platform for artists like Graham Parker and Joe Jackson. "Billboard launched Modern Rock Tracks, the magazine's first Alt Rock Chart. In September of 88."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Bleeding Edge and Mutation (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: At the start of the 1990s, alternative rock's "bleeding edge" was characterized by punk and post-punk, noise rock, and no-wave acts like Sonic Youth. This East Coast dissonance, combined with the metallic sludge from the Pacific Northwest, formed grunge, led by Nirvana. However, by late 1993 into 1994, alternative rock mutated, with bands like Nirvana on their *MTV Unplugged* set and Pearl Jam's *Vs.* showcasing quieter, more acoustic, rustic, and upbeat sounds, leading to a shift in mainstream preferences. "Punk and Post Punk, Noise Rock, and No Wave Acts like Sonic Youth were the bleeding edge of alternative rock at the turn of the 90s."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: A Little Love and Some Tenderness Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Breakthrough and Slacker Rock (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: Alternative music experienced a significant commercial explosion in the early 1990s, driven by the massive success of grunge bands like Nirvana, Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, and Alice in Chains. Below this mainstream success, a related style known as "Slacker Rock" emerged, characterized by its laid-back attitude and ragged edges, which often incorporated lo-fi aesthetics. "Alternative music had blown up thanks to the success of brunch. You know, Nirvana, ProJM, SoundGarden, Alton Chained, and so on. But below that was what some people called Slacker Rock, a style that was laid back while still being ragged around the edges."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Californian "Golden Generation" (1990s)
podcast.body: The early 1990s saw the rise of a "golden generation" of Californian alternative rock in the United States, a movement significantly influenced by bands like R.E.M. from their mid-to-late 1980s university concerts. This generation, featuring bands like Pixies, Mercury Rev, and Pavement, directly drew inspiration from R.E.M.'s pioneering sound. "con la nueva década en los 90 hace una generación dorada de música alternativa a rock en Estados Unidos liderada por los pigments."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: El papel de REM en los '80

podcast.title: College Rock Connection (Mid-1980s)
podcast.body: In the mid-1980s, "alternative rock" was often an interchangeable term with "college rock," particularly as campus radio stations began to gain significant influence in promoting new music. Independent labels, operating outside the mainstream major label system, embraced the loose, rough, raw, back-to-basics, primitive, cheap, and cheerful approach of these bands. This unfancy and reactionary style, sometimes distorted and wobbly, was considered cool and lent a specific context to the music, appealing to many listeners. "This was the era of college rock, which for a while was an interchangeable term with alternative rock. Some independent labels, companies operating outside the major label system and therefore offering an alternative really embraced this loose rough raw back-to-basics quasi-permative, cheap and cheerful approach."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Concept Evolution
podcast.body: The concept of alt-rock has evolved to the point where it may no longer exist as a distinct category. Instead, it is seen as simply "different flavors of rock," with varying levels of popularity, where any style has the potential to briefly enter the mainstream. "the concept of alt-rock no longer exists. It's just different flavors of rock with some being more popular than others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 15

podcast.title: Connected to Independent Labels
podcast.body: The term "alternative rock" is theorized to have derived from the practice of bands recording for small, independent record labels. For artists whose sound was considered too radical for major labels, these independent companies served as their only "alternative," hence the music they produced was labeled "alternative rock." "So therefore bands who recorded for these alternative labels made alternative rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dependence on Indie Scene
podcast.body: Several essential alternative rock movements, sounds, or trends could not have emerged without the foundational contributions of indie artists and indie labels, underscoring the critical role of the independent music ecosystem. "There were several essential alt rock movements or sounds or trends or whatever you want to call them that could not have happened without indie artists and indie labels."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Disdain for Video Practice
podcast.body: The alt-rock revolution brought artists who were largely disdainful of the industry practice of "We Must Make a Video" and were often openly hostile towards the MTV machine. This stance marked a fracture in the music video world, as these artists challenged the established norms of promotional video production. "These artists were largely disdainful of the whole We Must Make a Video Practice, and were often openly hostile to the MTV machine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 2

podcast.title: Dominance in Mid-90s
podcast.body: In the mid-1990s, the "alternative rock" tag was "all but guaranteed to dominate" the charts, characterized by elements like "grungy guitars, growly vocals, quirky lyrics." "Anything with that tag was all but guaranteed to dominate in the mid 90s."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Dominance in the 1990s
podcast.body: Alternative rock, initially kickstarted by Grunge, grew to dominate most of the 1990s music landscape, offering various genres beyond the mainstream. "But that music was just the kickstart for the alternative nation that came to dominate most of the 90s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Embrace of Unique Female Artists
podcast.body: Alternative rock provided a fertile ground for female artists who deviated from conventional norms in sound and appearance, often exhibiting bewildering senses of style, poise, and confidence. This genre, particularly with the openness of Gen Xers during the Grunge explosion, embraced musicians like Björk, who introduced different musical styles and kept music innovative. "when we slide into the world of alt rock, there are some women who sound like no one else."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution from New Wave
podcast.body: By the late 1980s, New Wave began to pivot towards what would become known as alternative rock. This shift saw formerly young artists, now in their 30s, resembling "Elder Statesmen" and, however unwittingly, appearing ahead of the curve by doing "whatever they wanted" musically. "as New Wave pivoted toward what became known as alternative rock, the formerly young men, all in their 30s, began to resemble Elder Statesmen."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Evolution to New Pop
podcast.body: By the end of the 1990s, "so-called alternative rock would become the new pop," a shift that Nirvana frontman Kurt Cobain could not have foreseen. "so-called alternative rock would become the new pop."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Factors in Alt-Rock Growth (Mid-1980s)
podcast.body: The expansion of the alternative scene in North America during the mid-1980s was significantly aided by college radio, bands actively touring alt-friendly clubs, independent record stores stocking unique music, and MTV's role in playing music videos from new UK bands. These elements collectively helped evangelize new fans and spread the movement. "Yes, college radio helped. So did all the bands willing to tour alt-friendly clubs and so did independent record stores, which set themselves apart from the big chains by stocking more of the weird stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: From "Left of the Dial" to Mainstream
podcast.body: Until the late 1980s, many forms of "Left of the Dial Rock" were deemed uncommercial or required commercial watering down for mainstream appeal. "Alternative Rock" was a deliberate distinction from both Top 40 pop and Album-Oriented Rock (AOR) artists like Van Halen. "It was called Alternative Rock because it was also distinguished from what got played on album-oriented rock or AOR radio stations."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Generational Appeal and Evolution
podcast.body: Alternative rock has been popular across multiple generations of fans and performers over the last 25 years. Current bands' sounds, attitudes, and images are shaped by their influences, with many famous acts frequently citing common names from the past that continue to shape future music. "Alternative rock has been around long enough so that it's been enjoyed by several generations of fans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Bauhaus?

podcast.title: Heritage of Mid-2000s Rock
podcast.body: The successful rock music of the mid-2000s, which ruled in the summer of 2005, was "music based on alt-rock heritage," with influences from the 90s alt-rock, 80s underground rock, and 70s punk. "Rock, and remember this is music based on alt-rock heritage, ruled."

podcast.title: Historical Scope
podcast.body: The history of alternative rock, as explored in this series, delves into every facet of the genre, tracing its origins from the 1950s right up to the present day. "So every Sunday you'll get a brand new episode of this series that examines every single facet of alt-rock from the 1950s right up to, well, pretty much today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Historical Series Overview
podcast.body: The "history of alt-rock series" is a 15-part deep dive examining every facet of alt-rock from the 1950s up to the present day. "We're going all the way back to this spring of 2010 and a 15-part deep dive into the history of alternative rockets, the history of alt-rock series."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: History Overview
podcast.body: The history of alternative rock spans from its pioneers in the 1950s and 60s, through explosions in the 1970s and early 80s, the "alt-rock nation" days of the 1990s, and the rise of indie rock in the early 21st century. It encompasses punk, new wave, grunge, Britpop, and indie movements. "We started all the way back in the 1950s and we tracked the early pioneers through the 60s and early 70s, followed by the explosion of the 1970s and early 80s, the alt-rock nation days of the 1990s and the rise of Indy Rock in the first decade of the 21st century."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 15

podcast.title: Identity Marker
podcast.body: In the late 20th century, a listener's identity was frequently "defined by what side of the mainstream versus alternative divide their tastes ran," contrasting sharply with the genre-fluid listening habits of younger generations (Y, Z, and Alpha). "a listener's very identity was defined by what side of the mainstream versus alternative divide their tastes ran."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Lo-Fi Influence and Authenticity (1980s-1990s)
podcast.body: The rise of alternative rock, often grouped with post-punk acts, saw artists inspired by the viability of home recording championed by figures like Bruce Springsteen. The genre prioritized capturing authenticity and realness, actively avoiding slickness and polished production. The practice of quickly creating music, dubbing it onto cassettes, and distributing or selling them at shows became a common approach. "This was an inspiration to several post-punk acts that were being grouped under the label of Alternative Rock. Again, capturing authenticity and realness was the goal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Long History of Revivals
podcast.body: The segment of the rock universe known as alternative rock has existed for nearly 50 years, and throughout this half-century, it has experienced numerous internal revivals where older sounds are rediscovered and re-fashioned. "We've been calling a certain segment of the rock universe alternative for almost 50 years now."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Longest Surviving Sub-culture
podcast.body: Goth is identified as one of the longest surviving alternative rock sub-cultures in the world. "Think of this as a beginner's guide to one of the longest surviving alternative rock sub-cultures in the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mainstream Takeover in Early 90s
podcast.body: Alternative rock began taking over the mainstream in the fall of 1992, coinciding with the release and commercial success of Stone Temple Pilots' debut album *Core* and hit song "Plush." "From the fall of 1992, right as alternative rock was taking over the mainstream, that Stone Temple Pilots and plush a huge commercial success, 10 million copies sold around the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mainstreaming Marginal Music
podcast.body: The mid-90s marked the peak of Generation X on the charts, which mainstreamed music previously considered "too marginal or weird for mass consumption," including bands from Butthole Surfers to Smashing Pumpkins. "The peak of Generation X on the charts was mainstreaming music that had previously been considered too marginal or weird for mass consumption."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: North American Tipping Point (Mid-1980s)
podcast.body: By the mid-1980s, the underground music scene in North America reached a tipping point, as enough people had discovered punk, new wave, and their associated subgenres. This led to increased clout for campus radio stations and a growing alternative scene, which attracted fans weary of mainstream rock. "It had taken a few years, but by the middle 1980s, the underground music scene in North America had reached some kind of a tipping point."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Outsider Camp in 70s-90s Rock
podcast.body: From the 1970s to the 1990s, Alternative Rock represented one of two dominant "tribes" in rock music. Its adherents were considered the outsiders, weirdos, and misfits, a position they were largely content with. They were engaged in a "cold war" with mainstream rock fans, where admitting to liking mainstream acts like Led Zeppelin or Black Sabbath was considered heresy. "On the other side were the alternative kids. They were the outsiders, the weirdos, the missfits, and they were quite happy with that position."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-1980s Complexity
podcast.body: After the 1980s, the history of alt-rock ceases to be a straightforward timeline, evolving into numerous subgenres, sub-subgenres, and even sub-sub-subgenres, requiring an approach that bounces between different scenes and sounds while trying to connect the underlying threads of alt-rock culture. "Now, if you can imagine our history of alt-rock as a timeline, we're now into the 1980s. But here's our problem. We can no longer chart the history of alt-rock with a nice straight line. More music, more sounds, more approaches, all means more subgenres, sub-subgenres, and even sub-sub-subgenres."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Boom Landscape
podcast.body: The period following the alternative rock boom saw the emergence of one-hit wonders, the "polarizing sound" of nu-metal, and the rise of electronica, creating a challenging environment that made the future look "pretty grim for guitar rock in general." "Left in its place was a spring of one-hit wonders, the polarizing sound of new metal, and the rise of Lectronica. And it honestly looked pretty grim for guitar rock in general back then."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Nirvana Era
podcast.body: Following Kurt Cobain's death in 1994, the subsequent "post-Grunge era" was characterized as "frothier, more commodified, often more cynical," yet also full of "unexpected twists." "The post-Grunge era that followed Cobain's passing would be frothier, more commodified, often more cynical, and yet also full of unexpected twists."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Rejection of the Fade-Out Technique
podcast.body: A key legacy of punk and New Wave, influencing alternative rock, was the shunning of the fade-out as a song ending technique. Bands like Pearl Jam and Nirvana, along with many other punk and alternative groups, opted for definitive beginnings and endings for their songs. "One of the legacies of punk in New Wave was the fact that the fader became shunned."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Ongoing History Book of Firsts

podcast.title: Shift from British to American Dominance
podcast.body: While British acts frequently topped the Modern Rock Chart in early 1993, the period's end saw the complete shift to American Grunge, signifying the "final transition from British to American Alt Rock." "1993 was also the final transition from British to American Alt Rock."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Shift in Ethos and Anti-Fashion
podcast.body: With the rapid growth of alternative rock, especially grunge, the entire ethos of music videos shifted. Glamour was out, replaced by an unpolished and authentic aesthetic. Fancy sets and costumes gave way to anti-fashion, and camera and band performances became central, often accompanied by an increased level of sincerity and irony. "Glamour was out, unpolished and authentic was in. Fancy sets and costumes were out, anti-fashion took over from fashion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 2

podcast.title: Sonic Youth's GU Album as a Hinge Point
podcast.body: The Sonic Youth album "GU" is considered a major turning point in the entire history of alternative rock. "A record that turned out to be a major hinge point in the whole history of alternative rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: SoundScan Impact on Charts
podcast.body: Alternative rock saw its fortunes boosted on the pop charts with the addition of SoundScan to Billboard's charts in 1991. The accurate sales data provided by SoundScan allowed alternative rock, along with country music and hip hop, to achieve better representation and higher positions on the Hot 100 than before. "Sound Scan boosted the fortunes of genres that had never done so well on the pop charts before, including country music. Hip hop and alternative rock."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Toppermost of the Poppermost Edition Part 1

podcast.title: The Smiths' Legacy
podcast.body: The Smiths are regarded as one of the most "magical bands" in the history of Alternative Rock, despite their relatively short career. Their enduring mystery and influence cemented their place in the genre's history. "this was one of the most magical bands in the history of Alternative Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Smiths

podcast.title: The Stooges' Influence
podcast.body: The Stooges were "absolutely bloody essential" in establishing the groundwork for the alternative rock movement that would unfold in the decades to come. "absolutely bloody essential in setting the stage for all the punk, alternative, and New Rock that was to come in the decades ahead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: The Velvet Underground as Pioneers
podcast.body: The Velvet Underground is widely considered by many music enthusiasts to be the inaugural true alternative rock band, highlighting their foundational influence on the genre. "Most music geeks, me included, considered them to be the first true alternative rock band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Umbrella for Diverse Sounds
podcast.body: Alternative rock functioned as an umbrella genre in the 1990s, encompassing a wide array of sounds including Goth, Industrial, Shoegaze, Lo-fi, and even singer-songwriters that didn't conform to mainstream rock conventions. "Once it pulled you into this universe, and you had a chance to look around, you realized that there were all kinds of new fresh, strange and fascinating sounds that existed under the umbrella of Alt Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Wilco's Significance
podcast.body: A live album from Wilco, recorded in 1996, is released for "lovers of American alternative music," indicating their importance within the genre. "para los amantes de la música alternativa americana."
